RAG, not fine-tuning, and it is not close for your case. Fine-tuning teaches a model style, format, and behavior; it does not reliably teach facts, and anything you bake in goes stale the next time an SOP changes. Retrieval keeps the source of truth in your documents where your ops lead can edit it.

What I would actually do first, in order:

- Collect the 20 or 30 questions your ops team is already asking ChatGPT. That is your test set, and it is the single highest-value hour in the project.
- Fix the documents before the model. Most SOP retrieval failures are document failures: three versions of the same policy, no dates, no owner, scanned PDFs with no text layer. Pick one authoritative copy of each.
- Build a small retrieval prototype over a single well-scoped domain, say dispatch or claims, not all SOPs at once. Chunk by section with the document title and effective date attached to every chunk.
- Make it cite. Every answer shows the SOP name and section, and says "I do not have that" when retrieval comes back weak. Citations are what turn ops skepticism into adoption.
- Measure against your question set before anyone else touches it.

Effort: a credible prototype over one domain is usually a few weeks of one engineer's time, not a quarter. The long pole is almost never the model, it is document cleanup and deciding who owns the answer when two SOPs disagree.

turns.assistant:
RAG, not fine-tuning, and it's not close for this use case. Here's why:

- Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into the model's weights at a point in time. Your SOPs change (new routes, new compliance rules, new vendors), so you'd be retraining constantly, and it's still a black box that can quietly hallucinate on anything outside its training data.
- RAG keeps your SOP docs as a live, searchable library the model reads from before answering. Update a doc, the answer updates. No retraining, and you can literally show the source paragraph it pulled from, which matters a lot in logistics where someone might quote this back to a customer or an auditor.
- Fine-tuning also needs a lot more labeled data and ML expertise to do well. RAG needs your documents to be reasonably organized and a modest amount of engineering.

What I'd actually do first, in order:
- Get your SOPs into clean, current text (this is usually the real work, not the AI part)
- Stand up a basic RAG pipeline: chunk the docs, embed them, retrieve relevant chunks per question, answer with citations back to the source doc
- Pilot it with a handful of ops people on real questions before rolling it out company-wide

Effort-wise, a working first version for a 40-person company is typically a matter of weeks, not months, assuming your docs aren't a mess. The docs being scattered or half-outdated is usually what stretches the timeline, not the AI itself.

First useful version:
- Pick one high-volume workflow and 20 to 50 approved SOPs.
- Clean ownership, versions, permissions, and effective dates before indexing.
- Build retrieval with section-level citations and links to the source.
- Require the assistant to abstain when evidence is missing or conflicting.
- Create 50 to 100 real ops questions, including ambiguous and outdated cases, then measure citation correctness and unsupported claims.
- Pilot with 5 to 10 users before connecting Slack, Teams, or other systems.

Under reasonable assumptions, a focused proof of value is roughly 2 to 4 weeks with one AI engineer and a part-time operations owner. A production-ready internal assistant is more often 6 to 10 weeks once authentication, access controls, document syncing, evaluation, monitoring, and feedback workflows are included.
